theme: True fasting; the Spirit’s anointing; Zion’s future glory
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 58:1-60:22. God describes the fast he wants, the Servant speaks about the Spirit’s anointing, and the future glory of Zion shines like sunrise. Read chapter 58 as a challenge, and chapter 60 as a promise.
settingTheScene: The last section of Isaiah, chapters 56 to 66, addresses a community that has begun to return from exile, or is on the verge of it, and finds the promised glory slow to appear. The people ask why God does not notice their fasting. The answer is that religion without justice is empty. Then the section moves on to the Spirit-anointed one, a new covenant, and a future in which the nations stream to the light of Zion.
observation: “Cry aloud; do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet; declare to my people their transgression” (58:1).
“Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free?” (58:6).
“Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house?” (58:7).
“Then shall your light break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up speedily” (58:8).
“Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save… but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God” (59:1-2).
“He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation” (59:16).
“And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression” (59:20).
“Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you” (60:1).
interpretation:
Chapter 58 begins with a surprise. The people seem religious, “seeking” God daily, delighting to know his ways. They fast, and they wonder why God does not see. God answers that on the day of their fast they pursue their own interests and oppress their workers. They fast with quarreling and strife. A day of bowing the head like a reed is not what God wants. The fast that he chooses is to set the oppressed free, share bread with the hungry, shelter the homeless, and clothe the naked. This is Isaiah 1 again. True worship cannot be separated from compassion.

The promise attached to this obedience is wonderful. “Then shall your light break forth like the dawn.” “You shall be like a watered garden.” And the Sabbath is also mentioned: delight in it, and God will cause you to ride on the heights of the earth.

Chapter 59 turns to the problem beneath. The LORD’s hand is not too short to save. It is sin that separates. The chapter is a bleak confession of corporate guilt: “Our transgressions are multiplied before you.” Justice is turned back, truth stumbles in the street. “He saw that there was no man… then his own arm brought him salvation.” God himself, a divine warrior, puts on righteousness as a breastplate and the helmet of salvation. “And a Redeemer will come to Zion.” A new covenant is promised: “My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart.”

Chapter 60 is a wave of light. Darkness covers the earth, but the LORD rises over Zion, and nations come to her light. Kings come to the brightness of her rising. Her gates are open continually. The sun and moon are replaced by the LORD as an everlasting light. “Your people shall all be righteous; they shall possess the land forever.” The people who were exiles become a glorious city.
connection: Jesus said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (Matthew 25:35-40). James 1:27 and 2:14-17 echo the call to practical compassion. Paul uses the armor of Isaiah 59:17 in Ephesians 6:14-17. Romans 11:26-27 quotes Isaiah 59:20-21 about the Redeemer. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and Revelation 21:23-25 shows the city lit by the glory of God, its gates never shut, and the nations walking by its light.
application:
Choose one concrete act of justice or mercy: share a meal, give to the poor, or help someone out of a hard situation.

Ask how your spiritual practices, such as fasting, prayer, and church, affect how you treat people.

Let the light of Christ shine in a dark place this week.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you the fast he chooses, and ask how you can share bread with the hungry.
Confess where your religion has been empty.
Ask him to let your light rise.
